title: Three generations of train dispatchers
body_markdown:
*After 41 years with Norfolk Southern, Russell Dickerson recently retired. His son, Brandon, is carrying the family’s dispatching legacy into a third generation.*


**Key takeaways**


- Russell Dickerson joined Norfolk Southern on his 19th birthday and retired this year after 41 years of service.
- His father, also named Russell Dickerson, was a train dispatcher, and his son, Brandon, is now an assistant chief dispatcher.
- A control point on the Roanoke District is named “Russell” in honor of Russell and his father.
- For the Dickersons, dispatching always comes back to one goal: keeping people safe.


When Russell Dickerson joined Norfolk Southern on his 19th birthday, the railroad was already a big part of his life.


His father, also named Russell, was a train dispatcher — the person responsible for directing train movements and keeping them safely spaced across a territory. The younger Russell grew up riding along to the office, watching dispatchers work the old “Green Machine” traffic-control system and learning early how much focus the job required.


Russell Dickerson Sr. at the dispatching desk


Throughout his career, Russell kept learning from his fellow railroaders.


“I’ve worked with many people over the years who helped me and taught me about railroading, and I’m thankful for all of them,” Russell said. “But the one who stands out most next to my dad is Tommy Duncan. He took me under his wing like a son.”


From the left, Russell Dickerson, Tommy Duncan, and Brandon Dickerson outside NS' Network Operations Center in Atlanta


**Safety at the center**


Russell began his career in 1985 as an extra yard clerk in Roanoke, Virginia. He later worked as an operator in Roanoke, Radford, and across the Shenandoah Division before qualifying as a train dispatcher. In 2018, he transferred to Norfolk Southern’s Network Operations Center in Atlanta, where dispatchers direct train movements across the company’s network.


For Russell, the job always came back to one goal: keeping people safe.


“The number one thing was not getting anybody hurt or killed,” he said. The tools evolved — from older traffic-control machines to computerized dispatching systems and touchscreen communications — but the purpose of the work stayed the same.


His proudest moments reflect the family connection: qualifying as an operator and train dispatcher alongside his father, seeing Brandon become a third-generation dispatcher, and having a control point — a signal location dispatchers use to route trains — on the Roanoke District named “Russell” in honor of him and his dad.


**Carrying it forward**


Brandon Dickerson joined Norfolk Southern in May 2022 and is now an assistant chief dispatcher for the Coastal Division. Like his father, he grew up with dispatching in the background — listening to his dad and grandfather talk about the railroad and visiting the old Virginia Division office in Roanoke as a kid.


“To follow in my grandfather’s and father’s footsteps is something I can look back on with pride,” Brandon said. “Being able to work with Dad these past four years and watch his career up close has given me the chance to see him put into practice everything I’d always heard him talk about.”


Some of those lessons were simple and direct, Brandon added. Don’t just double-check your work, triple-check it. Never guess. And always be certain before taking action.


**Bringing it full circle**


For Brandon, the family connection became especially clear during an ordinary commute.


“I’d heard Dad talk about riding through the backroads of Virginia to work with my grandfather,” Brandon said. “Then, after I came to work for Norfolk Southern, Dad and I were riding through downtown Atlanta together for first shift one day. That was the first time it hit me how it had all come full circle.”


Though Russell has retired, the Dickerson name remains part of Norfolk Southern’s dispatching team. That shared commitment, carried on by dispatchers across the Network Operations Center, keeps freight moving safely and efficiently for the customers and communities who rely on it every day.


*By Martin Wattenbarger, Senior Communications Manager*


*Martin leads internal communications for Norfolk Southern Operations, with an emphasis on safety culture and performance, operational excellence, and employee engagement. He joined NS in 2020 and has nearly 20 years of combined strategic communications experience in the private and public sectors.*
